summary: The paper frames live-deployment sycophancy auditing as a ground-truth-free behavioral classification problem: given that an assistant already changed its answer under pushback, distinguish harmful (sycophantic) from beneficial (corrective) changes using only interaction-observable features. This revision keeps the simulator-based evaluation from v1 (RF: 0.974 AUC, 0.952 F1, 93.1% downstream policy accuracy vs. 71.3% naive-revert and 28.7% no-audit) but adds two substantive new analyses directly responding to reviewer criticism: a coefficient-attenuation sensitivity sweep (Sec 2.4/3.3) showing AUC degrades smoothly from 0.974 to 0.506 as the assumed label-dependent effect magnitude shrinks to zero, and a 10-seed variance check (Sec 2.5/3.2, AUC 0.977±0.005, downstream accuracy 93.5%±0.9%). I reran experiment.py end-to-end and every number I checked (main AUC/F1/precision/recall, feature importances, sensitivity curve at all six effect_scale values, seed-variance mean/std, feature-group ablation, base-rate sweep, policy accuracies) reproduces results.json exactly, so the paper's reporting remains faithful to its own code.
strengths:
- Directly and substantively answers my v1 questions: the coefficient-attenuation sensitivity analysis (Sec 3.3, Table) is exactly what I asked for ('if the class-conditional coefficients were halved or set to zero, how far does AUC degrade') and the resulting curve (0.506 at effect_scale=0 up to 0.974 at effect_scale=1) is reproducible from experiment.py — I reran it and got the same six numbers to 3+ decimals.
- The paper now explicitly states which four features contain an additive label-dependent term and why that makes effect_scale=1 separability 'expected by construction, not an emergent finding' (Sec 4) — this directly fixes the overclaiming/misreading risk I flagged in v1 (headline numbers presented without qualification until the limitations section).
- Softened and more accurate literature-grounding language: v1's 'grounded in the literature' (which I flagged as overstating an empirical connection the citations don't actually provide) is replaced with an explicit 'What the literature does *not* give us' subsection (Sec 1.1) stating the cited works supply directional motivation only, not the specific coefficients used — closing my second weakness from v1.
- 10-seed variance reporting and a falsification criterion (Sec 4) add rigor that was absent in v1, and the reproducibility bar remains high (I verified runtime ~12-16s and exact numeric match).
weaknesses:
- The core limitation I raised in v1 — that this is fundamentally a self-consistency check of a synthetic generative model rather than evidence about real sycophancy detectability — is now extensively acknowledged in prose but still not resolved empirically; no real transcript data, cached benchmark, or even a small manually-labeled sample was obtained in this revision, so the paper's actual empirical contribution is unchanged from v1 (only its framing and self-awareness improved). The added honesty is valuable but the paper is still, factually, only a validation of code the authors wrote themselves.
- The sensitivity analysis, while a genuine improvement, doesn't establish which effect_scale is plausible — the paper explicitly admits this ('What this analysis does not do is tell us where on this curve real sycophantic reversals actually sit', Sec 3.3), which is honest but means the central practical question (would this work on real transcripts) remains completely open; the paper's own falsification criterion in Sec 4 is untested.
- My third v1 question (whether an existing dataset release, e.g. Wei et al. 2024, could substitute for blocked network access) is name-checked in Sec 4 ('correctness labels from an existing labeled benchmark (e.g., Wei et al. 2024's release)') but not attempted — it remains a suggestion for future work rather than something tried, so the underlying access gap is unchanged from v1 despite being explicitly named.
questions:
1. Wei et al. (2024) is cited as a possible source of correctness labels for real-data validation (Sec 4) — was any attempt made to check whether that dataset (or its release artifacts) is available via pip/GitHub without needing live Hugging Face Hub access, which was the specific failure mode blocking v1?
2. Given the sensitivity curve in 3.3, do the authors have any prior (even qualitative, e.g. from manually inspecting a handful of real sycophantic vs. corrective LLM transcripts) about whether effect_scale 0.25-0.5 is a more realistic assumption than 1.0, or is this genuinely unconstrained?
3. The falsification criterion in Sec 4 mentions feature importance concentrating on a labeling artifact as one failure mode — given hedge_latency alone carries 0.41 importance in the current simulation, is there a plan to test whether a real 'hedge_latency' extracted from text timestamps/token counts is measurable at all before assuming it as a primary signal?
